Section 1.2 of Lock⁵ asks the question behind every statistic: **how were the
data collected?** A *population* is the collection of all cases we want to
understand, while a *sample* is the subset we actually measure. A statistic
computed from a sample can be generalized to the population only when the
sample was selected **randomly** — a *simple random sample* gives every set of
*n* cases the same chance of being chosen. Non-random methods (voluntary
response, convenience samples, haphazard picking) invite **sampling bias**, and
even a random sample can be ruined by a leading question, nonresponse, or
untruthful answers. Two properties of a statistic matter: its *bias* (does it
hit the population value on average?) and its *variance* (how much does it
bounce from sample to sample?) — randomness is what keeps both under control.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 27–31). Skill Builders 1.34–1.51 drill the definitions,
1.52–1.56 ask “is it biased?”, and the rest apply the ideas to real studies;
tabs based on Lock5 data files include a small executable EDA.

## Exercise 1.34

**To estimate the size of trout in a lake, an angler records the weight of 12
trout he catches over a weekend.**
*(Skill Builder 1: population or sample?)*

- **Sample.** The 12 trout caught are a subset of all the trout in the lake.
  The sample mean weight of the 12 fish would be a statistic used to estimate
  the population mean weight of all trout in the lake.

## Exercise 1.35

**A subscription-based music website tracks its total number of active users.**

- **Population.** The website tracks *every* active user, not a subset — the
  count is a parameter, computed from the whole population of users.

## Exercise 1.36

**The US Department of Transportation announces that of the 250 million
registered passenger vehicles in the US, 2.1% are electro-gas hybrids.**

- **Population.** The percentage is computed from *all* 250 million registered
  passenger vehicles — the entire population — so 2.1% is a parameter, not a
  statistic from a sample.

## Exercise 1.37

**A questionnaire to understand athletic participation on a college campus is
emailed to 50 college students, and all of them respond.**

- **Sample.** The 50 students are a subset of the campus community. Since all
  50 responded there is no nonresponse bias, but the data still describe only
  a sample of the population of all students at the college.

## Exercise 1.38

**A sociologist conducting a survey at a mall interviews 120 people about
their cell phone use.**
*(Skill Builder 2: describe the sample and a reasonable population.)*

- **Sample:** the 120 people interviewed at the mall.
- **Reasonable population:** all people who shop at that mall (perhaps more
  broadly, people who shop at malls). Because mall patrons are a convenience
  sample, generalizing beyond mall shoppers would be risky.

## Exercise 1.39

**Five hundred Canadian adults are asked if they are proficient on a musical
instrument.**

- **Sample:** the 500 Canadian adults questioned.
- **Reasonable population:** all Canadian adults.

## Exercise 1.40

**A cell phone carrier sends a satisfaction survey to 100 randomly selected
customers.**

- **Sample:** the 100 randomly selected customers (strictly, those who
  respond).
- **Reasonable population:** all customers of the cell phone carrier.

## Exercise 1.41

**The Nielsen Corporation attaches databoxes to televisions in 1000 households
throughout the US to monitor what shows are watched and produce the Nielsen

- **Sample:** the 1000 US households with databoxes on their televisions.
- **Reasonable population:** all US households with televisions.

## Exercise 1.42

**To estimate the proportion of Americans who support changing the drinking
age from 21 to 18, a random sample of 100 college students are asked “Would
you support a measure to lower the drinking age from 21 to 18?”**
*(Skill Builder 3: (a) sample, (b) population of interest, (c) population we can generalize to.)*

- **(a) Sample:** the 100 college students.
- **(b) Population of interest:** all Americans.
- **(c) Generalize to:** college students — particularly students at similar
  colleges. College students likely view the drinking age differently than the
  general adult population.

## Exercise 1.43

**To estimate the average number of tweets from all Twitter accounts in 2019,
an author randomly selected 10 of his followers and counted their tweets.**

- **(a) Sample:** the 10 followers who were selected.
- **(b) Population of interest:** all Twitter accounts in 2019.
- **(c) Generalize to:** the author's followers (people who follow this
  particular account) — nothing broader.

**To investigate interest across all residents of the US in a new type of ice
skate, a random sample of 1500 people in Minnesota are asked about their
interest.**

- **(a) Sample:** the 1500 people in Minnesota.
- **(b) Population of interest:** all residents of the US.
- **(c) Generalize to:** residents of Minnesota — perhaps people living in

## Exercise 1.45

**To determine the height distribution of female high school students, the
rosters are collected from 20 randomly selected high school girls basketball
teams.**

- **(a) Sample:** the members of the 20 sampled girls basketball teams.
- **(b) Population of interest:** all female high school students.
- **(c) Generalize to:** female high school basketball players — basketball

## Exercise 1.46

**The population is incoming students at a particular university. Each name is
thrown into a hat, the names are mixed, and 20 names (each corresponding to a
different student) are drawn.**
*(Skill Builder 4: random sample or not?)*

- **Random sample.** Every student has an equal chance of being drawn, the
  names are mixed, and no student is listed twice — this is a simple random
  sample.

## Exercise 1.47

**The population is the approximately 25,000 protein-coding genes in human
DNA. Each gene is assigned a number from 1 to 25,000, and software randomly
selects 100 numbers, yielding a sample of 100 genes.**

- **Random sample.** Numbering the population and letting software pick the
  numbers is exactly the technology-based equivalent of drawing names from a
  hat.

## Exercise 1.48

**The population is all employees at a company. All employees are emailed a
link to a survey.**

- **Not a random sample** (as described). Inviting everyone is an attempt at a
  census, not a random selection of a subset. The eventual sample consists of
  whoever chooses to respond — a voluntary response sample — and there is no
  guarantee it represents all employees.

## Exercise 1.49

**The population is adults between the ages of 18 and 22. A sample of 100
students is collected from a local university, and each student at the
university had an equal chance of being selected.**

- **Not a random sample from the given population.** Only students at the
  local university can be chosen, so adults aged 18–22 who are not students
  there have no chance of being included. The sample is random within the
  university's students, but that is a different population.

## Exercise 1.50

**The population is all trees in a forest. We walk through the forest and pick
out trees that appear to be representative of all the trees.**

- **Not a random sample.** This is a haphazard, judgment-based selection;
  human choice tends to oversample some kinds of trees (big, healthy, easy to
  reach) and undersample others.

## Exercise 1.51

**The population is all people who visit the website CNN.com. All visitors are
invited to take part in the daily online poll.**

- **Not a random sample.** Everyone is invited, but the sample consists only
  of visitors who volunteer to click — a classic voluntary response sample.

## Exercise 1.52

**Ask a random sample of students at the library on a Friday night “How many
hours a week do you study?” to estimate the average for all college
students.**
*(Is it biased?)*

- **Biased.** Students found at the library on a Friday night are plausibly
  the campus's heaviest studiers — people who study little are elsewhere. The
  estimate of average weekly study hours would almost certainly be too high.
  A random sample only removes sampling bias if it is drawn from the whole
  population of interest, not from a subgroup.

## Exercise 1.53

**Ask a random sample of people in a school district, “Excellent teachers are
essential to the well-being of children in this community, and teachers truly
deserve a salary raise this year. Do you agree?”**

- **Biased.** This is a leading question: the wording stacks the deck in favor
  of agreement before the respondent answers. The estimated proportion
  supporting a raise would be inflated (wording bias, not sampling bias).

## Exercise 1.54

**Take 10 apples off the top of a truckload of apples and measure their
bruising to estimate average bruising for the whole truckload.**

- **Biased.** The 10 apples are not randomly selected — they come from one
  convenient location. Bruising is likely to differ by position in the load
  (apples on top were loaded last; apples at the bottom bear the weight of the
  pile), so the top-of-the-load sample is not representative.

## Exercise 1.55

**Take a random sample of one type of printer and test each printer to see
how many pages it will print before the ink runs out; use the average to
estimate the average for all printers of this type.**

- **Not biased.** The sample is randomly selected from exactly the population
  of interest (printers of this type), so the sample average is a reasonable
  estimate of the population average — provided the printers are tested under
  the same conditions.

## Exercise 1.56

**Email a random sample of students at a university asking whether the
university should fund an ultimate frisbee team; a small number reply, and
the replies are used to estimate support among all students.**

- **Biased.** Even though the initial sample was random, only a small,
  self-selected group replied. Students who care about ultimate frisbee are
  far more likely to respond, so the estimated support would be inflated —
  a nonresponse / voluntary response bias.

## Exercise 1.57

**Do Parents Regret Having Children?** The *Kansas City Star* selected a
random sample of parents from Kansas City and asked “If you had it to do over
again, would you have children?” In this sample, 94% said “Yes.” To what
population can this statistic be generalized?

- To **parents in Kansas City** — that is where the random sample was drawn.
  Randomness earns generalization only as far as the sampling frame: the 94%
  is a trustworthy estimate for Kansas City parents, not for all parents in
  the US. (Recall Data 1.4: a voluntary write-in poll of parents gave 30%,
  while a random national sample gave about 91%.)

## Exercise 1.58

**Wearing a Uniform to Work.** The website fox6now.com held an online poll
asking “What do you think about the concept of having an everyday uniform for
work, like Steve Jobs did?” Of the people who answered, 24% loved the idea,
58% hated it, and 18% already wore a uniform to work.

- **(a)** Unlikely. This is a voluntary online poll: respondents choose
  whether to participate, so people with strong opinions about uniforms are
  overrepresented, and the audience is limited to visitors of one local news
  website.
- **(b)** No. Because the respondents are self-selected and non-representative,
  the 24% cannot be generalized to all adult workers.

## Exercise 1.59

**Canadians Stream Music.** In a random sample of 3500 Canadian consumers,
about 71% report that they regularly stream music.

- **(a)** Yes, likely. The consumers were *randomly selected* from the
  population of Canadian consumers, so the sample should be representative
  (barring nonresponse or untruthful answers).
- **(b)** Yes. With a random sample it is reasonable to estimate that about
  71% of all Canadian consumers regularly stream music; the true percentage
  should be close to the sample percentage.

## Exercise 1.60

**Climate Change.** In June 2018, a poll asked a random sample of 1000 US
adults whether global warming will be a serious problem for the United States:
51% said very serious, 27% somewhat serious, and 21% not serious.

- **(a) Sample:** the 1000 US adults polled. **Intended population:** all US
  adults.
- **(b)** Yes. Since the sample was randomly selected from US adults, it is
  reasonable to estimate that about 21% of all US adults think global warming
  will not be a serious problem.

## Exercise 1.61

**Do You Use a Food Delivery App?** A 2019 eMarketer study asked 800 US
smartphone users whether they had used a food delivery app at least once in
the last month; 16.3% had. Of those, 27.6% used DoorDash, 26.7% Grubhub, 25.2%
UberEats, and the rest another app.

- **(a) Sample:** the 800 US smartphone users surveyed. **Intended
  population:** US smartphone users (the population to whom eMarketer wants to
  speak is smartphone users, roughly US adults with smartphones).
- **(b) Cases:** the 800 smartphone users. **Variables:** whether the person
  used a food delivery app in the last month (yes/no) — **categorical**; and,
  for users, which app was used (DoorDash / Grubhub / UberEats / other) —
  **categorical**. Note the second variable is recorded only for the subset
  who answered yes.

## Exercise 1.62

**Pennsylvania High School Seniors.** `PASeniors` contains a random sample of
457 Pennsylvania Grade-12 students drawn by the US Census at School website
from students who matched those criteria between 2010 and 2019. For each
group below, discuss whether generalizing the sample results would be
reasonable.

- **(a) The 457 students in the original sample:** trivially yes — statistics
  such as the sample mean describe these 457 cases exactly; no generalization
  is needed.
- **(b) All Pennsylvania high school seniors who participated in the Census at
  School survey:** reasonable. The 457 were randomly selected from exactly
  this group, so results generalize well to it.
- **(c) All Pennsylvania high school seniors:** more questionable. Only
  seniors whose schools/teachers opted into Census at School can be sampled,
  and participation is voluntary — participants may differ systematically
  (more engaged in math and science projects, for example) from seniors who
  never took part. Generalize with caution.
- **(d) All students in the United States who participated in Census at
  School:** no. The sample is restricted to Pennsylvania and to Grade 12;
  students in other states and grades had no chance of being included.

*Data:* `data/ch01/PASeniors.csv` (n = 457, 36 variables), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/PASeniors.csv>.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pas = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/PASeniors.csv")
pd.DataFrame({"Survey year": pas["Year"].value_counts().sort_index()})
```

The sample spans the 2010–2019 window of the Census at School project; every
case is a Pennsylvania student who chose to participate — the boundary of
generalization discussed above.

## Exercise 1.63

**How Easily are You Influenced?** Asked to mentally simulate ten tosses of a
fair coin by writing H's and T's, over 80% of a random sample of people wrote
Heads as the first flip. When the instructions said “Tails and Heads,”
participants were more likely to start with Tails; with a purple/orange
imaginary coin, they started with whichever color was mentioned first.

- **(a)** This is **wording bias, not sampling bias** — the sample itself was
  random. The bias enters through how the question presents the options: the
  first option mentioned is preferentially chosen (the primacy effect).
  (People are also simply bad at simulating randomness.)
- **(b)** Present **Option W first**. Since people gravitate to the first
  option listed, leading with W stacks the choice in favor of the option you
  hope they pick.

## Exercise 1.64

**Does Chocolate Milk Come from Brown Cows?** A US National Dairy Council
survey appeared to show that 7% of Americans (about 16.4 million people)
believe chocolate milk comes from brown cows; the sampling method was never
made public.

- **(a)** We cannot know. Without knowing how the sample was determined we
  cannot judge whether generalizing to all Americans is appropriate, and a
  dairy advocacy group hoping for a fun, shareable headline had every
  incentive to produce a striking number. Plausible biasing schemes include
  an opt-in online poll, or sampling only from audiences likely to joke
  around (e.g., a comedy-show audience), either of which would inflate the
  “brown cows” percentage.
- **(b)** Yes — the wording invites bias. Respondents were forced to choose
  among “(a) Brown cows, (b) Black and white spotted cows, (c) I don’t know”:
  both real options are cows, “I don’t know” nudges people to guess between
  them, and no “other” option is offered. A fairer wording would be
  open-ended — “Where does chocolate milk come from?” — allowing answers such
  as “from cows, with chocolate flavoring added” or “none of the above.”

## Exercise 1.65

**How Many People Wash Their Hands after Using the Washroom?** Harris
Interactive researchers stood in public restrooms (at Turner Field in
Atlanta, Penn Station and Grand Central in New York, the Museum of Science
and Industry and Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, and the San Francisco Ferry
Terminal) pretending to comb their hair while observing patrons. Of over 6000
people observed, 85% washed; 93% of women and 77% of men.

- **(a) Cases:** the 6000+ restroom patrons observed. **Variables:** whether
  the person washed their hands (yes/no) — **categorical**; gender —
  **categorical**; the restroom/location where the person was observed —
  **categorical**. All variables as recorded are categorical.
- **(b)** In the telephone survey over 96% claimed they always wash, versus
  85% actually observed. People do not answer truthfully about embarrassing
  behavior: they report what they *should* do, not what they *do* (social
  desirability bias). Observation does not depend on the subject's candor,
  which is exactly why the two numbers differ so much.

## Exercise 1.66

**Teaching Ability.** In a sample survey of professors at the University of
Nebraska, 94% described themselves as “above average” teachers.

- **(a) Sample:** the University of Nebraska professors surveyed. **(b) —
  population:** all professors at the University of Nebraska.
- **(b)** No. Nothing above suggests the professors were selected in a biased
  way; the sample comes from the group of interest. The red flag here is not
  sampling bias.
- **(c)** No. It is logically impossible for 94% of teachers to be above
  average. The professors' self-ratings are not truthful measures of teaching
  ability — most people rate themselves favorably — so the statistic measures
  self-image, not the quantity it claims to estimate.

## Exercise 1.67

**Effects of Alcohol and Marijuana.** In 1986 the Australian Federal Office of
Road Safety tested combinations of alcohol and marijuana on mood and
performance. Participants were volunteers who responded to advertisements on
two rock radio stations in Sydney; each volunteer was given a randomly
determined combination of the two drugs. Is the sample likely representative
of all Australians?

- **No.** The sample consists of self-selected volunteers from the audience of
  two Sydney rock stations — plausibly younger, more risk-tolerant, and more
  interested in drugs than the average Australian. Note the randomization was
  in *assigning treatments*, which supports causal conclusions, but says
  nothing about *how the sample was chosen* — that was no random sample of all
  Australians. At best, results generalize to similar young adults who would
  volunteer for such a study.

## Exercise 1.68

**What Percent of Young Adults Move Back in with Their Parents?** The Pew
Research Center polled a random sample of n = 808 US residents aged 18–34; 24%
had moved back in with their parents for economic reasons after living on
their own. Is this a representative sample of all US residents aged 18–34?

- **Yes, likely.** The sample was randomly selected from exactly the target
  population (US residents aged 18–34), so it should be representative of that
  group. As always, the estimate also depends on truthful answers and
  manageable nonresponse, but the method of selection itself is sound.

## Exercise 1.69

**Do Cat Videos Improve Mood?** Dr. Jessica Gall Myrick posted an online
survey on Facebook and Twitter about feelings before and after the last cat
video watched; everyone who clicked and completed it was included. Over 6000
people completed the survey, generally reporting more energy and more positive
emotions afterwards.

- **(a)** No. This is a self-selected (voluntary response) sample of people
  who happened to see the link and chose to complete it — not a simple random
  sample from any defined target population.
- **(b)** Several other bias channels: cat lovers are overrepresented among
  those who click; the questions rely on recall and self-report of mood;
  the wording of the questions can shape answers; and links spread through
  networks of like-minded friends, compounding the selection bias. People
  also may not accurately remember or admit their moods.

## Exercise 1.70

**Diet Cola and Weight Gain in Rats.** Rats fed yogurt sweetened with a
zero-calorie artificial sweetener gained more weight and body fat than rats
fed sugar-sweetened yogurt. News articles implied that people who drink diet
soda gain more weight. Explain why we cannot conclude that.

- The study was on **rats, not people**. Even a flawless experiment on rats
  only establishes cause and effect for rats; metabolism differs between
  species, so the result cannot automatically be generalized to humans. (The
  experiment itself was well designed — the issue is the leap from rats to
  people, not the internal validity.)

## Exercise 1.71

**Armoring Military Planes.** In WWII the US military recorded bullet holes on
B-24 bombers that returned from missions; most holes were in the wings and
tail, so the military proposed armoring those regions. Abraham Wald argued
instead for armoring the *center* of the plane. What was his argument?

- **Survivorship bias.** The sample includes only planes that *made it back*.
  Holes in the wings and tail show places a plane can be hit and still return;
  planes hit in the center (engines, cockpit) never came back to be counted.
  The *missing* data — the absent holes in the center of returning planes —
  reveal where hits are fatal, so that is where armor belongs.

**Employment Surveys.** US employment statistics rely on the Current

status, job type, and demographics of each resident, and the Current
Employment Statistics (CES) survey, sampling 140,000 nonfarm businesses and
government agencies for payroll jobs, pay rates, and related information.

- **(a) CPS population:** all US households (the residents of the United
  States living in households).
- **(b) CES population:** all nonfarm businesses and government agencies in
  the US.
- **(c)**

    the cases).
  - ii. What percentage of Americans are self-employed? → **CPS** (people in

## Exercise 1.73

**National Health Statistics.** The CDC's NHANES interviews and examines a
random sample of about 5000 people in the US each year; the NHAMCS collects
information from hospital records for a random sample of individuals treated
in hospital emergency rooms.

- **(a)** NHANES findings generalize to the **US population** (people living
  in the US).
- **(b)** NHAMCS findings generalize to **emergency room visits in the US**
  (people treated in hospital emergency rooms), not to the general population.
- **(c)**
  - i. Are overweight people more likely to develop diabetes? → **NHANES**
    (needs a sample of people, not ER visitors).
  - ii. What proportion of ER visits involve sports-related injuries? →
    **NHAMCS**.
  - iii. Difference in average ER waiting time between male and female
    patients? → **NHAMCS**.
  - iv. What proportion of US residents have visited an ER in the past year? →
    **NHANES** (a random sample of US residents can simply be asked).

## Exercise 1.74

**Interviewing the Film Crew on Hollywood Movies.** There were 1295 movies
made in Hollywood between 2012 and 2018. For a documentary, a random sample of
5 movies will be selected for in-depth crew interviews. Assuming the movies
are numbered 1 to 1295, use a random number generator to select the sample.

- Number the movies 1–1295 and let the generator pick five numbers; the
  movies with those numbers are the sample. With seed 2026 the selected
  numbers, matched to the Lock5 `HollywoodMovies` file, are:

*Data:* `data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv` (n = 1295), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HollywoodMovies.csv>.

```{python}
#| echo: false
hm = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv")
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
picks = np.sort(rng.choice(np.arange(1, 1296), size=5, replace=False))
sel = hm.iloc[picks - 1][["Movie", "Genre", "AudienceScore", "Year"]].copy()
sel.insert(0, "Number", picks)
sel
```

Every set of five movies has the same chance of being chosen — this is a
simple random sample. Different samples give different statistics: with 10,000
replications of “sample 5 movies and average their AudienceScore,” the
statistic centers on the population mean but bounces from sample to sample,
which is the sampling variability Chapter 3 will quantify.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Sampling distribution of the mean AudienceScore over 10000 random samples of 5 movies"
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
pop = hm["AudienceScore"].dropna().to_numpy()
means = np.array([pop[rng.choice(len(pop), size=5, replace=False)].mean()
                  for _ in range(10000)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.hist(means, bins=40, color="#4c72b0", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(pop.mean(), color="#c44e52", lw=2,
           label=f"Population mean = {pop.mean():.1f}")
ax.axvline(means.mean(), color="#55a868", lw=2, ls="--",
           label=f"Mean of sample means = {means.mean():.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean AudienceScore in a sample of 5 movies")
ax.set_ylabel("Samples")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"center (mean of 10000 sample means) = {means.mean():.2f}; "
      f"spread (std dev) = {means.std():.2f}")
```

## Exercise 1.75

**Sampling Some Starbucks Stores.** The Starbucks chain has about 24,000
retail stores in 70 countries. A member of the administration wishes to visit
six stores, randomly selected. Suppose the stores are numbered 1 to 24,000;
use a random number generator to select the numbers for the 6 stores.

- Number the stores 1–24,000 and select six *distinct* numbers (a store
  visited twice would waste a visit, so we sample without replacement). With
  seed 2026:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
stores = np.sort(rng.choice(np.arange(1, 24001), size=6, replace=False))
pd.DataFrame({"Store number (1-24000)": stores})
```

These six numbers identify the stores to visit. Each store — and each set of
six stores — has the same chance of being chosen, so the sample is a simple
random sample of the chain's stores.

:::
